title: Specht Modules and the Irreducibles of the Symmetric Group

items.title: Column antisymmetrizers, polytabloids, and Specht modules
items.statement: For λ⊢n, n≥0, and a λ-tableau t, put κ_t=Σ_{γ∈C_t}sgn(γ)γ in C[S_n] and e_t=κ_t{t} in M^λ. Define S^λ to be the complex span of all e_s for λ-tableaux s. Sign on permutations of {1,…,n} is transported from the published finite-symmetric-group sign convention by relabelling; S_0 and the empty tableau give κ=e={t}=1 and S^∅=C.
items.proof_strategy: Define the finite signed sum using the column stabilizer and tabloid basis. The shift i↦i−1 preserves inversion pairs, so the 1-based sign agrees with the published finite-ordinal sign. Show C_t∩R_t={1}; hence distinct γ∈C_t give distinct tabloids γ{t}, and the coefficient of {t} in e_t is 1, so every e_t is nonzero. The next covariance lemma establishes stability and cyclicity.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Chapter 3, Definition 3.8, printed p. 12
David A. Craven, Groups, Geometries and Representation Theory, Sections 1.8 and 2.1, printed pp. 16-22

items.title: Polytabloid covariance and the column sign rule
items.statement: For every λ-tableau t and σ∈S_n, κ_{σt}=σκ_tσ^{-1} and e_{σt}=σe_t. If γ∈C_t, then γe_t=sgn(γ)e_t. Consequently S^λ is an S_n-submodule of M^λ and is generated by any one e_t.
items.proof_strategy: First absorb Chan's column-factorization lemma inline: use the direct product of the column symmetric groups and multiplicativity of sign to factor κ_t as the product of the column antisymmetrizers. Conjugate C_t using the published tableau-stabilizer lemma and use conjugation invariance of parity to obtain the κ formula. Apply it to σ{t} for covariance. Reindex the antisymmetrizer sum under multiplication by γ∈C_t to get the sign eigenrelation. Transitivity of S_n on λ-tableaux then makes every e_s a translate of e_t, proving both stability and cyclicity, including n=0.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Lemmas 3.10-3.11 and Definition 3.12, printed p. 13

items.title: Invariant Hermitian product on a tabloid module
items.statement: For every λ⊢n, give M^λ the Hermitian product ⟨Σ a_s{s},Σ b_s{s}⟩=Σ over tabloids s of conjugate(a_s)b_s, conjugate-linear in its first argument. The tabloid basis is orthonormal, the form is positive definite and S_n-invariant, and each κ_t acts self-adjointly.
items.proof_strategy: Use the finite tabloid basis to define the form. S_n permutes this basis, hence its action is unitary. For γ∈C_t, γ* =γ^{-1} and sgn(γ^{-1})=sgn(γ), so κ_t*=κ_t. Positivity over C, rather than mere nondegeneracy of an ambient bilinear form, is the property used later.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Chapter 9, Definition 9.1 and Remark 9.2, printed pp. 31-32; the Hermitian version is defined and checked locally
David A. Craven, Groups, Geometries and Representation Theory, Section 2.1, printed pp. 19-20

items.title: Column collision cancels antisymmetrization
items.statement: Let t have shape λ and let {s} be a μ-tabloid of the same n. If two entries a,b lie in one row of s and in one column of t, then κ_t{s}=0.
items.proof_strategy: The transposition τ=(a b) belongs to C_t and fixes {s}, because it only permutes entries within a row. Choose coset representatives g for C_t/⟨τ⟩ and write κ_t=Σ_g sgn(g)g(1−τ). Each summand annihilates {s}; this also works in characteristic zero without any assumption on λ or μ.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Chapters 3-4, printed pp. 12-17
David A. Craven, Groups, Geometries and Representation Theory, Sections 1.8 and 2.1, printed pp. 16-22

items.title: Nonzero antisymmetrizer image detects dominance
items.statement: For λ,μ⊢n and a λ-tableau t, if κ_t M^μ is nonzero, then λ dominates μ in the published order λ⊒μ.
items.proof_strategy: Use linearity on the μ-tabloid basis: a nonzero image means some tabloid {s} has κ_t{s}≠0. The collision lemma then forces every row of s to meet every column of t in at most one entry. Apply the basic combinatorial lemma to obtain λ⊒μ, including n=0; the witness argument is an existence proof and uses no choice principle.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Theorem 4.1(a) and proof, printed p. 15

items.title: The antisymmetrizer image in its own tabloid module is one-dimensional
items.statement: For every λ⊢n and λ-tableau t, κ_t M^λ=C e_t, and e_t≠0.
items.proof_strategy: The coefficient-one term gives e_t≠0. For each basis tabloid {s}, either κ_t{s}=0, or the column-collision lemma implies the row-column incidence hypothesis of the basic combinatorial lemma. Its equal-shape clause gives ρ∈R_s and γ∈C_t with ρs=γt, hence {s}=γ{t}. Reindex the signed sum directly to prove the needed right group-algebra identity κ_tγ=sgn(γ)κ_t, so κ_t{s}=sgn(γ)e_t. Linearity gives κ_tM^λ⊆C e_t; e_t=κ_t{t} gives the reverse inclusion.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Lemma 2.14 and proof, Definition 3.8, Lemma 3.11(b), and Theorem 4.1(b), printed pp. 9-10, 12-13, 15

items.title: James's submodule theorem over the complex numbers
items.statement: For λ⊢n and any S_n-submodule U⊆M^λ, either S^λ⊆U or U⊆(S^λ)^⊥, where orthogonality is for the invariant Hermitian tabloid product.
items.proof_strategy: If some u∈U and λ-tableau t have κ_tu≠0, the one-dimensional-image lemma gives κ_tu=c e_t with c≠0; U is a linear subspace stable under every element of S_n, so the finite group-algebra sum κ_tu lies in U, hence e_t∈U, and cyclicity gives S^λ⊆U. Otherwise κ_tu=0 for every u,t. Self-adjointness yields ⟨u,e_t⟩=⟨κ_tu,{t}⟩=0 for every t; the e_t span S^λ, so U⊆(S^λ)^⊥. In this positive-definite complex setting the alternatives are in fact exclusive, since S^λ is nonzero and has zero intersection with its orthogonal complement.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Chapter 9, Definition 9.1, Remark 9.2, Lemma 9.3 and proof, and Theorem 9.4 and proof, printed pp. 31-32; the local product is Hermitian

items.title: Complex Specht modules have nondegenerate Hermitian self-pairing
items.statement: For every λ⊢n, S^λ is nonzero and S^λ∩(S^λ)^⊥={0} for the positive definite invariant Hermitian tabloid product.
items.proof_strategy: Use the canonical row-filled tableau from the permutation-module definition; the coefficient of its tabloid in e_t is 1, so S^λ contains a nonzero vector. Apply the orthogonal-complement definition to v∈S^λ∩(S^λ)^⊥ with the same v in both slots; positive definiteness forces v=0. Do not infer this from nondegeneracy of the ambient bilinear form alone, which does not restrict nondegenerately to every complex subspace.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Chapter 9, Definition 9.1, Remark 9.2 and Lemma 9.3, printed pp. 31-32; the local form is Hermitian
David A. Craven, Groups, Geometries and Representation Theory, Section 2.1, Corollary 2.4 and its characteristic-zero conclusion, printed p. 20; the local proof uses Hermitian positivity

items.title: Complex Specht modules are irreducible
items.statement: For every n≥0 and λ⊢n, the nonzero complex S_n-representation S^λ is irreducible.
items.proof_strategy: For a nonzero S_n-submodule U⊆S^λ, use the Specht submodule inclusion S^λ⊆M^λ to view U as a submodule of M^λ and apply James’s dichotomy. If U⊆(S^λ)^⊥, then U⊆S^λ∩(S^λ)^⊥=0, contradiction. Thus S^λ⊆U, whence U=S^λ. The self-pairing lemma supplies S^λ≠0, including at n=0.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Theorem 4.4(b) and proof, printed p. 16; Theorem 9.4 and complete proof of the submodule dichotomy, printed pp. 31-32

items.title: Homomorphisms from Specht to Young permutation modules obey dominance
items.statement: For λ,μ⊢n over C, a nonzero S_n-map φ:S^λ→M^μ implies λ⊒μ. At μ=λ, every S_n-map S^λ→M^λ is a scalar multiple of the inclusion; equivalently Hom_{C[S_n]}(S^λ,M^λ)=C.
items.proof_strategy: Maschke supplies an S_n-stable complement T to S^λ in M^λ. The projection p along T is equivariant and is the identity on S^λ; set Φ=φ∘p. If φ is nonzero, the polytabloids span S^λ, so some t has φ(e_t)≠0. Equivariance and e_t=κ_t{t} give φ(e_t)=Φ(κ_t{t})=κ_tΦ({t})≠0, hence κ_tM^μ≠0 and λ dominates μ. When μ=λ, the one-dimensional-image lemma gives φ(e_t)=c e_t with c≠0, and cyclic generation gives φ=c times the inclusion on all of S^λ. The zero map is zero times the inclusion; the inclusion is nonzero because a canonical polytabloid has coefficient one. Thus Hom is one-dimensional and canonically isomorphic to C.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Chapter 4, Theorem 4.1(a-b) and proof, Corollary 4.2(a-b) and full proof, Theorem 4.3 (Maschke), and Theorem 4.4(c) and proof, printed pp. 15-16

items.title: Distinct complex Specht modules are inequivalent
items.statement: If λ,μ⊢n and S^λ≅S^μ as complex S_n-representations, then λ=μ.
items.proof_strategy: Take an equivariant isomorphism f. A canonical nonzero polytabloid shows i_μ∘f:S^λ→M^μ is nonzero; the composite is equivariant and hence a C[S_n]-module map, so the preceding Hom-dominance theorem gives λ⊒μ. Prove f^{-1} equivariant and repeat with i_λ∘f^{-1} to get μ⊒λ. Antisymmetry of dominance yields λ=μ. Check both composites are nonzero on the canonical polytabloids.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Theorem 4.4(a) and complete proof, printed p. 16
Mark Wildon, Representation Theory of the Symmetric Group, Corollary 4.4 and proof, printed p. 15

items.title: Specht modules classify the complex irreducibles of S_n
items.statement: For every n≥0, the modules {S^λ:λ⊢n} form a complete irredundant list, up to isomorphism, of finite-dimensional irreducible complex S_n-representations.
items.proof_strategy: Audit and establish the finite-group and field hypotheses for the published class-count theorem: S_n is a finite group, C is algebraically closed, and its characteristic is zero because the embedded ordered field R has no positive natural multiple of 1 equal to zero. Its order is positive since it contains the identity, so zero does not divide |S_n|. The preceding irreducibility and inequivalence results define an injective map from partitions of n to irreducible isomorphism classes. Explicitly biject cycle-type tuples with partitions by listing c_k copies of k, including the empty tuple/partition at n=0; combine this with the published cycle-type class result and the class-count theorem to get equal finite cardinalities. The image of the injective map is a subset of the finite class set of irreducibles with the same cardinality, hence is the whole set.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Corollary 4.5 and its proof, printed p. 16; the proof refers to Theorem 4.4 and Lecture 2's first corollary
Pavel Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory, Theorem 3.5 and Corollary 3.6 with proof, printed pp. 33-34

items.title: Tabloid and column orders for Specht straightening
items.statement: Fix λ⊢n. Order λ-tabloids by declaring {u}>{v} when the largest label placed in different rows is in a lower row of u than of v. A tableau is column-standard when each column increases downward. Order column-standard λ-tableaux by u≺v when the largest label placed in different columns is farther left in u than in v. Both are finite strict total orders; the unique empty tableau is their sole size-zero element.
items.proof_strategy: Each tabloid determines a row-index vector for labels 1,…,n; reverse lexicographic comparison of those vectors gives the first total order. Each column-standard tableau is uniquely determined by the column assigned to each label, since entries in each column are sorted; reverse lexicographic comparison gives the second. Fix the directions exactly so column permutations lower tabloid order, while Garnir exchanges increase column order.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Definition 4.8 and Remark 4.10, printed pp. 16-17
Mark Wildon, Representation Theory of the Symmetric Group, Definitions 6.3 and 6.9, printed pp. 26-27 and 30; the column order is reversed here for increasing Garnir induction

items.title: Leading tabloid of a column-standard polytabloid
items.statement: For a column-standard λ-tableau t, e_t has coefficient 1 at {t}, and every other tabloid in e_t is strictly below {t} in the fixed tabloid order. Consequently the standard polytabloids are linearly independent.
items.proof_strategy: The intersection C_t∩R_t is trivial, so each γ∈C_t contributes a different tabloid and identity contributes coefficient 1. For nonidentity γ, let m be the largest moved label. In the column-standard t, the entry γ^{-1}(m)<m lies above m in its column, so after γ acts, m lies in a higher row while every larger label stays in the same row. Hence {γt}<{t}. Distinct standard tableaux have distinct tabloids because their rows are sorted; taking the largest leading tabloid in a putative linear relation forces its coefficient to vanish.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Definition 4.8, Remark 4.10 and Theorem 4.11 proof, printed pp. 16-17
Mark Wildon, Representation Theory of the Symmetric Group, Proposition 6.5, printed pp. 27-28

items.title: Adjacent-column Garnir relation over C
items.statement: Let t be a λ-tableau. Let X lie among entries of column j and Y among entries of column j+1, with |X|+|Y|>λ′_j. Put H=S_X×S_Y, choose representatives T containing 1 for the left cosets gH in S_{X∪Y}, and G_{X,Y}=Σ_{g∈T}sgn(g)g. Then G_{X,Y}e_t=0 in M^λ over C.
items.proof_strategy: Let A_Z=Σ_{h∈S_{X∪Y}}sgn(h)h. In every tabloid term γ{t} of e_t, the entries X∪Y still occupy at most λ′_j rows, so some two lie in one row. Pair terms of A_Z by their transposition to obtain A_Zγ{t}=0 and hence A_Ze_t=0. Factor A_Z=G_{X,Y}A_H using the chosen left-coset representatives. Since H⊆C_t and h e_t=sgn(h)e_t, A_H e_t=|H|e_t; divide by the nonzero complex number |H| to get G_{X,Y}e_t=0. The factor ordering is for the library’s left action.

references.title: Mark Wildon, Representation Theory of the Symmetric Group, Definition 6.6, Example 6.7 and Theorem 6.8, printed pp. 28-30; theorem translated from the source's right action to the library's left action over C

items.title: Garnir straightening spans the complex Specht module
items.statement: Every λ-polytabloid is a finite complex linear combination of standard λ-polytabloids, for every λ⊢n, without using the later RSK identity.
items.proof_strategy: Column-sort arbitrary tableaux with the column sign rule. For a nonstandard column-standard tableau, take the least adjacent descent and construct X,Y. Use the canonical left-coset transversal indexed by p-subsets of X union Y, with each representative made from increasing-matched disjoint swaps, to isolate the identity term. Every nonidentity term sorts to a later tableau in the local order because its greatest changed label moves right under the left action. Finite reverse induction proves spanning over C, including the empty shape, using the local Garnir relation and without the later RSK identity.

references.title: Mark Wildon, Representation Theory of the Symmetric Group, Definition 6.9 and Lemma 6.10 with proof, printed pp. 30-31; Wildon's order is reversed in the local definition, and the source's right-action Garnir step is adapted using the proved left-action relation over C

items.title: Standard polytabloids form a basis of a complex Specht module
items.statement: For every λ⊢n, {e_t:t is a standard λ-tableau} is a C-basis of S^λ. In particular dim_C S^λ=f^λ, including dim S^∅=1.
items.proof_strategy: Prove independence using the leading-tabloid lemma. For spanning, express every Specht generator as a finite complex linear combination of standard polytabloids using the proved Garnir straightening lemma; use the local span characterization to obtain equality of spans. Use the standard-tabloid definitions to show the indexing family has exactly f^λ distinct members, and the finite-basis dimension definition to conclude dim_C S^λ=f^λ. Check the unique empty tableau and empty-shape polytabloid directly. Do not use the later RSK identity.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Theorem 4.11 and proof, Remark 4.13, printed pp. 16-17; the local spanning proof uses Garnir straightening instead of Chan’s later RSK count
Mark Wildon, Representation Theory of the Symmetric Group, Theorem 6.2, Proposition 6.5, Theorem 6.8, Definition 6.9 and Lemma 6.10 with proof, printed pp. 26-31

title: Specht Modules and the Irreducibles of the Symmetric Group — Examples

items.title: Polytabloids of shape (2,1)
items.statement: In M^(2,1), let v_i be the tabloid whose second row is {i}, i=1,2,3. For t=[1 2;3] and u=[1 3;2], the two standard polytabloids are e_t=v_3−v_1 and e_u=v_2−v_1. Every (2,1)-polytabloid is one of ±(v_3−v_1), ±(v_2−v_1), ±(v_3−v_2), and e_t,e_u form a basis of S^(2,1).
items.proof_strategy: List the three tabloids v_1,v_2,v_3. Each column stabilizer has the identity and the transposition exchanging the two first-column labels; calculate its two signed tabloid terms. The six tableaux yield the three differences and their negatives. The two standard tableaux give independent vectors (and the standard-basis theorem confirms they span).

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Remark 3.9 and its explicit shape-(2,1) polytabloid calculations, printed p. 12
Mark Wildon, Representation Theory of the Symmetric Group, Definition 2.4 and Example 2.6(B), printed pp. 5-6

items.title: The row and column Specht modules
items.statement: For n≥1, S^(n) is the one-dimensional trivial complex representation of S_n, while S^(1^n) is the one-dimensional sign representation. For n=0, S^∅ is the one-dimensional trivial representation of S_0.
items.proof_strategy: For the single row, each column has one entry, so C_t is trivial, κ_t=1, and the unique tabloid is fixed by S_n. For the single column, C_t=S_n, the singleton-row tabloids {σt} are distinct, and e_t=Σσ sgn(σ){σt} has coefficient 1 at {t}; reindexing by ρ=τσ computes τe_t=sgn(τ)e_t. Cyclic generation shows the Specht space is this nonzero line. Treat n=0 as the empty tableau, whose Specht space is C and whose acting group is trivial.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Definition 3.8, Lemma 3.11(b), and Example 3.14(a-b), printed pp. 12-14

items.title: All three Specht modules of S_3
items.statement: For S_3 the partitions (3),(2,1),(1^3) give Specht modules of dimensions 1,2,1 respectively: trivial, the sum-zero subspace of the natural three-point permutation module with basis v_3−v_1 and v_2−v_1, and sign. They are all the complex irreducibles.
items.proof_strategy: Use the previous two examples for explicit models. In the ordered basis a=v_3−v_1, b=v_2−v_1 of S^(2,1), calculate (12)a=a−b, (12)b=−b, (23)a=b and (23)b=a; these generate the standard two-dimensional action. Count the two standard (2,1) tableaux or read the basis theorem for dimension 2. Invoke the classification theorem only after the three concrete modules and their distinct dimensions/actions are displayed.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Example 3.14(a-b), printed p. 14; Theorem 4.4 and Corollary 4.5, printed pp. 16-17

items.title: A reducible Specht module in characteristic two
items.statement: Over F_2 form the (3,1)-tabloid permutation module with basis v_1,…,v_4 and its Specht subspace by the same signed column-antisymmetrizer formula. It is the 3-dimensional augmentation subspace W={Σ a_i v_i:Σ a_i=0}, and its nonzero invariant line F_2(v_1+v_2+v_3+v_4) is proper. Thus this modular Specht module is reducible.
items.proof_strategy: Define the F_2 construction explicitly, since the A-page Specht definition has complex coefficients. For shape (3,1), every polytabloid is v_i−v_j and all such differences span the kernel of the coordinate-sum map, of dimension 3. In characteristic 2, w=v_1+v_2+v_3+v_4 has coordinate sum 4=0, so w∈W; w is fixed by S_4 and spans a one-dimensional proper submodule. This directly witnesses failure of the complex irreducibility assertion if its field hypothesis is removed.

references.title: Charlotte Chan, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Remark 4.6, printed p. 16 (modular warning; the concrete F_2 example is computed here)
Mark Wildon, Representation Theory of the Symmetric Group, Examples 2.3(2) and 2.6(B), printed pp. 5-6 (hook-shape tabloids and polytabloids over a field; the reducibility witness is computed here)
